issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Minh Tran was a 44-year-old married nurse who had grown up in a South Eastern Asian family and had spent most of his adult life trying to be the kind of man who stayed calm, helpful, and dependable. Before the attack, his work had given him a familiar rhythm: long shifts, quick decisions, and the quiet satisfaction of moving through hospital corridors with purpose. The mugging happened on an ordinary evening after work, when he was walking to his car. He was approached suddenly, and in the few terrifying moments that followed, the world narrowed to hands, movement, and the sense that he had been chosen as an easy target. Even now, Minh described the event as if it were preserved in separate frames. When he tried to speak about it, he did not tell it as a smooth story; he referred to it in fragments, as though he were looking at photographs in his mind. What came back most clearly were pictures and images: the attacker’s presence, the position of the street, the sense of being trapped in place. He said that when the memory returned, it was not only visual. He felt it in his body again, with physical pain in the same parts of him that had hurt during the mugging, as if the scene were being replayed inside his muscles and ribs rather than merely remembered.

In the months that followed, Minh’s days began to fill with small acts of vigilance. He kept his mind occupied all the time, not because he felt energetic but because any pause left him alone with what had happened. At work, he found himself scanning every environment for signs of threat. He noticed exits immediately, watched who came in and out of waiting areas, and looked over his shoulder more than once when walking through dim parking structures or across the hospital lot after a late shift. He had also started checking mirrors repeatedly, including the rearview mirror in his car and reflective surfaces as he moved through corridors, because he needed to know who was behind him and whether anyone seemed to be following. That sense of danger followed him into ordinary routines. He always chose where to sit based on how safe or protected he felt, preferring seats that left his back covered or gave him a clear view of the room. In restaurants, family gatherings, and break rooms at the hospital, he would sit with visible caution, scanning around him before settling, then checking again if his attention drifted.

Sleep became difficult. Minh described lying awake at night, unable to fall asleep or staying asleep only lightly, waking alert and immediately orienting himself to the room. Even in bed beside his wife, he found himself listening for movement and replaying the scene in pictures. He did not say he was startled by loud sounds or crowds; instead, he described a more constant unease, a body that would not let go. During the day, he tried to blunt the impact by keeping himself mentally busy, but the vigilance never fully left. In the hospital, where he once moved with confidence, he now monitored hallways and faces with a seriousness that felt exhausting. On his commute home, he chose routes and parking spots with an eye to protection, and he was more likely to circle back or look behind him before unlocking the car. These habits had gradually changed how he moved through his life. He was still functioning, still showing up for work and family, but with more effort and less ease, and his wife had noticed how often he seemed to be somewhere else even when he was physically present.

As Minh spoke about the aftermath, what stood out most was the meaning he had come to give the event. He had become certain that there was something about him that made it happen. The thought did not sit as a vague fear; he voiced it as a conviction that he had somehow been marked out, made vulnerable in a way others were not. From there, his view of the future had darkened. He said nothing good can happen to me anymore, and he spoke about his life with a sense of finality that was painful to hear. He had come to believe he had no future, at least not the kind he once imagined. Those thoughts were now part of the way he interpreted ordinary moments: a glance from a stranger, a car slowing nearby, a darkened corridor at work, the act of sitting down in a public place. Each could become a cue for checking, scanning, or looking behind him.

By the time he sought help, Minh was not coming because the attack felt distant; he came because it still felt close enough to shape every day. He was tired of living as if another ambush might happen at any moment, tired of the sleepless nights and the constant internal effort of staying ahead of threat. He hoped, cautiously, that therapy might help him feel less trapped by the memory and less certain that his future was already lost, though what frightened him most was that the attack had changed something fundamental in him that could not be undone.
